analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers file income tax returns directly through the IRS website for free, without paid software.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to build a system letting individual taxpayers file their federal income tax returns electronically straight through the IRS website, with no paid intermediary. The IRS would run a public education campaign and report to Congress twice a year on progress. Today, most people who e-file must go through commercial software companies or preparers, which either charge a fee or steer them toward paid add-ons.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of individual taxpayers who now pay for tax software or preparation fees, or spend time navigating commercial 'free file' offers with income limits and upsells, would be able to file directly with the government at no charge.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Treasury Secretary to let individual taxpayers e-file federal income tax returns through the IRS website 'without the use of an intermediary,' phased in within three years of enactment.
It authorizes whatever funding is needed to run the program and requires a public information and consumer education campaign to encourage taxpayers to use it.
The IRS would consult with nonprofit taxpayer groups and report to Congress every six months on implementation and annually on taxpayer usage.

analysis.who_pays: Tax preparation and tax software companies would lose fee revenue from tens of millions of returns, and the government would bear the cost of building and operating the direct filing system.

drawbacks.text: Building and maintaining a government e-filing system would require ongoing appropriations, an open-ended amount under the bill, and the IRS would take on a new technology and support role it does not currently perform itself.

The commercial Free File program already provides free electronic filing to many taxpayers through private companies, so supporters of the status quo argue a government-run alternative duplicates an existing option — though Free File has income limits and routes taxpayers through commercial sites.
Taxpayers with complicated returns would still likely need commercial software or a professional preparer, since the bill only guarantees direct filing capability, not filing advice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and concrete: filing is a task nearly every household must do annually, and a free direct government option would remove fees and upselling for millions of people. The costs are real but modest relative to that — a federal technology program and lost revenue to the tax prep industry. The bill was thin on operational detail (it left design to the Treasury Department), which is a fair criticism, but not a reason it never even got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Akaka introduced the Free Internet Filing Act on March 29, 2007, joined by Sen. Jeff Bingaman.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax preparation and tax software companies, whose fee revenue from electronic filing was left untouched. Ordinary taxpayers who would have gained a free direct filing option got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Daniel Akaka
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Two Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans joined.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never brought the bill to committee action during the 110th Congress.

against.name: Tax preparation and software industry
against.role: Commercial e-file and tax software providers (e.g., Intuit, H&R Block)
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed IRS-run direct filing because it would compete with paid preparation and software products.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so no roll-call record exists; it had only Democratic sponsorship, and the Finance Committee, chaired by a Democrat, took no action either way.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software companies
industries.note: A direct IRS filing option would compete directly with paid software like TurboTax and paid preparers, which collect fees from tens of millions of returns each year. The industry's interest in blocking this runs against taxpayers who want a free way to file.

industries.industry: Free File intermediaries (IRS-contracted private filing platforms)
industries.note: The bill allows free filing either directly through the IRS or through intermediaries 'contracted by the IRS to provide free universal access,' so contractors could keep a role. But it would no longer funnel taxpayers through commercial sites with income limits and upselling, reducing the intermediaries' gatekeeping role.
